utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The witness has made it relevant and I could have no confidence that my learned colleague would not take it up in re-examination. I have to deal with it in cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you said the witness gave it relevance, you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The waving around of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed. The objection is denied.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now I appreciate that you tell us that you can understand that to give us some examples if you imagine being in their shoes, I think by mid-1992 with the first of the severe food shortages, is that correct, around June?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was around June, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Okay. It wouldn't have been very pleasant if you were a Sarajevan learning that UNPROFOR headquarters were about to pull out of Sarajevo and relocate to Zagreb, would it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably not but they didn't know that was going to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Are you saying in June they didn't know it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: By June, the headquarters had already withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: When were they told?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well they saw the headquarters withdraw on the 16th and 17th of May, they saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: So when you earlier said they wouldn't have known, would you at least agree with me that by July they knew?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly by July they knew that the major part of the headquarters had gone.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yeah. My point is that from the perspective of a citizen in Sarajevo, they would feel abandoned by that, wouldn't they?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: They might do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And they might do quite reasonably, mightn't they? I am not saying they were abandoned but they might reasonably conclude that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: We still had a significant -- I mean in July we had a significant UN presence in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Right. Now, another example and I'll move on, was there an incident where Mrs. Plavsic's mother was transported by the UN from within Sarajevo, within the confrontation lines, to Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: We attempted to do it but it wasn't successful.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Was it not successful because there was an angry demonstration outside her residence when it was attempted?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true. My soldiers actually -- my officers actually stood between the crowd and Mrs. Plavsic and protected her with their lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Okay. There might be some confusion here. I'm not talking about Mrs. Plavsic, I'm talking about Mrs. Plavsic's mother?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No I have no knowledge about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Are you not aware that General MacKenzie ordered that the UN transfer Mrs. Plavsic's mother from within the confrontation lines to where Mrs. Plavsic lived at Ilidza on the Bosnian Serb side of the confrontation lines?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. That wouldn't have looked particularly --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can a break be made between question and answer, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That would not have looked particularly good from the perspective of a hungry Sarajevan stuck in the city and being shelled, would it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In fact, was the UN referred to after that on the streets of Sarajevo as the Chetnik taxi service?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now -- excuse me, Mr. President. You will now see, I think, the video you have in mind in relation to the market shelling. Can we please have the other videotape played, I think the exhibit number is P3793 and just before its shown, I'll distribute the transcript. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, would you mind telling us what number of transcript it is?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Six. I'm sorry, the clip is six. If you could tell me the words on the tape, that might help me one was Mercedes and the other was -- bread, yes, that's it. Yes might that be played as soon as you're ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Who was the UN gentleman being interviewed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was Fred -- oh, I can't remember his last name, he was the -- basically the PR person for the UN headquarters in the PTT.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: We see on this report that, according to the commentator, there were eyewitnesses from the PTT building. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no eyewitnesses. It was close to the PTT, that's what the report said.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Okay. I stand corrected. Excuse me. I think the commentator said people watching from the nearby UN headquarters said it was difficult to believe it was not directly targeted. They're the words that were spoken?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. And it seems that at that stage it was thought to have been 105 millimetre shell; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And did you recognise the voice to be Kate Adie?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you know whether she was spoken to as to where she got her information from?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you know whether the film crew who were there seemingly within a minute or so, perhaps, were spoken to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What I'm suggesting to you is that a little bit of knowledge is a dangerous thing?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's very true, particularly with the media who put judgements on things that they have no right to.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Might the witness be shown Exhibit P3797?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Sir, this is a page from the book by Martin Bell titled "In harm's way" talking about his time in Sarajevo. I will read the last two paragraphs you can follow it in the text, "I noted self-critically that for weeks at a time" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace you know when reading there's always a tendency of speeding up.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please suppress that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: "During the years of working from Sarajevo, we would venture no further than the airport in one direction and the Presidency in the other. Our measure of Bosnia was approximately the length of a single street in its capital. Forays into Serb-land would be day trips only, usually unrewarding, and therefore attempted less frequently. In this self-critical mode I would ask myself, when had we ever shown a civilian victim of sniper fire on the Serb side of the lines? When had we reported from their hospitals? When had we heard from the Sarajevo Serbian News in Grbavica rather than Oslobodneje the celebrated newspaper on the government side which was an icon of journalism and a symbol of the city's ordeal? Even to raise these questions is to risk being branded as an apologist for the Serbs which I am not and never was. They started this war. They killed and they burned and they ethnically cleansed and the greater part of responsibility for it will always be theirs. But they didn't hold monopoly rights on evil. There were massacres also by Croats, and even by Muslims, and villages burned by both. The Serbs were demonised by themselves as well as by others. But such is the nature of television that some of the coverage of the war was quite literally weighted against them." Mr. Gray, they are not the words of someone who was blinded to the perspective of the Bosnian Serbs, are they?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they're not, but I mean he comes out to be quite equally weighted with both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you mean by that that in your mind, the Bosnian Presidency was more to blame, in a general sense, than the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not. I believe that there was equal blame.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You see, I suggest to you that that passage I've read is not consistent with your view of Martin Bell and your view of the BBC reporters generally in terms of impartiality?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was written in hindsight it was not written immediately at the time. I mean this book was written after he had been there and he was Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. wounded and he was removed. The actual reporting at the time, at the precise time and the blame that was placed on certain events was immediate, it was passed by satellite dish and they got it wrong on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember that when I showed you -- when I played to you your own tape of the Sir Douglas Hurd incident, Martin Bell was heard to say at the end of that segment, "The time and place of it suggested it was stage-managed by someone and it gave more force to Mr. Hurd's appeal for a cease-fire."

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: He didn't say, "This is the responsibility of the Serbs."

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Please wait. And he didn't say, "This is the responsibility of the Presidency," did he?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but what he did say was it was stage-managed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: But as to who did it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he -- he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: He didn't say?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't, no, no, you're quite correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. All right. Now, you told us that you met General Galic, when did you first meet him? Do you have a copy of your statement?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in August.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Well, take out a copy of your statement and please turn to page 10. I believe you -- first of all, do you have your statement in front of you now?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And did you make your statement in May of 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Would you please turn to page 10?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have done.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: These words appear, "After 13 July - about halfway down the page - or towards the end of July, General Sipcic no longer attended any meetings and General Galic took over from him as the Sarajevo corps commander. I then had negotiations with Galic over the extra containment sites without any form of warning. Sipcic just disappeared. I asked my liaison officer but never established where he had gone." So as of May, 1995, you thought that you met General Galic for the first time towards the end of July 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The end of July, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And at that stage, when you met him you understood him to be the Sarajevo corps commander; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You told us three days ago that you saw him every other day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was about every other day, yes, we had meetings when there was a requirement for cease-fires or I wanted to negotiate the next agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Okay. For whatever reason, every other day. Did he become a friend?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he wasn't a friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Were you able to communicate with him without an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you, when you came to Bosnia-Herzegovina, know even one word of Serbian?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: How did you come by that knowledge?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- as part of my pre-deployment training, I was given some training on the Serbo-Croat language.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Before you commenced that training, did you know one word of Serbian?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: We have heard evidence in this trial that General Galic didn't become the corps commander until about the 10th of September, 1992, that is, ten days before you left. What do you say about that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that either I'm wrong or someone else is wrong but I mean I've got it recorded in that statement and I've got it written in a notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is not challenged by either parties that this date is an accepted date and I do not know why if this is admitted and this is accepted, I do not see why that is a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, that was entirely inappropriate to say in front of the witness and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that the relevance is not about the date Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. primarily. The objection is denied, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I think it was clear to everyone that it was not about the date. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Are you now looking through a notebook?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just looking through because I know that I've got --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. Gray, please stop. I take it the answer is yes, you are looking through a notebook?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That's a different notebook to the one we saw the other day, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Have you shown that notebook to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: When did you do that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I first arrived here.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did they make a copy of it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. You've now come to a page which I think I can see from here has the corner turned up; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Might I have access to the notebook.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course. You can have access to any of the documents I have here.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you remember the other day I asked you about the documents that you've got there, Mr. Gray? Do you remember we talked about that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, and I offered to actually pass them across to you and you could have them. That was at the end of the session.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You didn't mention this notebook, did you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned the documents that I had. That is part of the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, this particular --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, it's the recollection of the Chamber that the witness expressed himself in such terms that everything he would have with him would be available for the Court, the trial, the parties so he made a very general offer.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I can respond to that first.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'd like to see this notebook because I did not see it myself and I do not know whether this is in a telephone book or what. I did not see it so could I please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... before continuing, may I ask you one thing, you said you don't know whether the Defence copied this notebook. Did you give it to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I passed across a whole range of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mean I've got a -- my briefcase is full of documents here. I passed across all the videotapes, I passed across computer discs, I passed across CD-ROMs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I understand, I do understand everything.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not aware that they didn't actually get that. I'm not aware of that because it's got a lot of names and contact details and telephone numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just ask you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any reason for you that among the materials you gave to the Defence, this booklet was not included?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: An oversight on my part, that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I'm not suggesting to you that you did not do or that you did do but do you have any reason to believe that among the whole bunch of material you transferred to the -- you gave to the Defence, that this would not have been in it or would you expect it to have been in it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no reason -- as I said, it's got a list of names in it, contact details. I probably didn't think that it was really important but it does have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand your answer correctly that you did not give it to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not think I did. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please Mr. Ierace, before putting questions to the witness, could you just pass the document to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Might I finish looking at it first, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President. As Mr. Ierace needs some time, could we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you what, I'm listening to the French?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Could we have the schedule?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we are -- if I would -- we are almost at the time where the Prosecution would have used the same time as the Defence. It's a bit difficult to give a precise calculation because of many incidents during cross-examination whereas the examination-in-chief was with less incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm in your hands as to how we deal with this. I only intend to -- in the interests of saving time to confine my questions to the one page which simply says, "COL stop --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, before, I mean this is highly inappropriate, this is highly improper. We need to see it first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, Mr. Ierace indicates what he would like to do. I indicated before that the document should be passed to the Defence. I take it that Mr. Ierace wanted to say that at this moment he wanted to confine himself to questions in relation to a certain page and he would then have passed it to you but you give him no opportunity to follow the orders I'd given previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I said that it's absolutely inappropriate to start reading out this text and start quoting from it without being able to comply with your instructions and without the Defence and General Galic being able to see it. This is what is totally inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Piletta-Zanin. If you read that page and have a look through the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, might I ask questions in relation to that page and no other?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You want to restrict yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, I do in the interests of saving time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and then meanwhile, the Defence can -- you may put your questions in respect of that one page.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that it could be read in half a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The only words that appear on that page are colonel, spelled C-O-L. Stanislav Galic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: There's no other pen marks on that page, are there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there aren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: There's no date printed or otherwise?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. It could be important those aren't the only words that are there it could be important and I'll provide this to the Trial Chamber. I don't know if it's relevant or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for the sake of the transcript, the -- Mr. Ierace, you did put to the witness that the only words readable on this page were Colonel abbreviated, then Stanislav Galic, the word "Stanislav" appears just above a word stricken out which is still legible which says "Slavoljub."

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: How does that page assist you in determining that you first met General Galic towards the end of July 1992?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because if you look at the -- at the position of the page, it's towards the end of the book or the -- the notepad and you'll see a lot of names and telephone numbers that appear before it so I mean it's -- purely an indication of, if you like, a timeline of when he actually appeared in Sarajevo and that is not my handwriting, that is the handwriting of someone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Who? Who?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's one of my interpreters who wrote it down.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, approximately how many times did you meet General Galic, in other words, more than 10 more than 20, less than 100 if you could give us some idea?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Less than 100 and certainly more than 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Can you be any more specific than somewhere between 10 and 100?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot. Our meetings were determined by the war and the availability of General Galic and the opportunity to actually meet him. He was a busy man and it wasn't just a matter of you just arrived and you could have a meeting. There was no point in having meetings --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Please stop. You told us the other day that the Bosnian Serb side showed you all of their heavy weapons; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: They showed me most of them. They actually gave me a guided tour of all their heavy weapon positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: How do you know that they showed you most of them?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know but I know that they showed me a large number of weapons which weren't under UN supervision and they were quite freely -- they were quite happy under the terms of the second agreement to have those weapons that they did show me put under UN supervision.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. You don't know but you assume that they did; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, may I remind you that there's not much time left. Could you finish in ten minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I will try, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The workshop under the PTT, when did that close down?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was still operating when I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I suggest to you that's incorrect?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I was aware, on the 20th of September, it was still operating.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Were there times when the UN staff took refuge in the basement during shellings?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And was that on the same floor as the workshop?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Was the workshop -- how many floors were there underground?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were through sublevels, the first sublevel was the one where the UN took cover during shelling, the second sublevel was the workshop, the third sublevel was the car park, underground car park where we had our UN vehicles parked.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Sir, it was hardly secret when the BBC could not only film it but film it in operation, was it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's very true. The BBC were camped on our front doorstep. There was a small office directly on the very, very ground level -- I mean if you look at the PTT building, there's a large ramp which goes up and covers the sublevels and then you basically got a large open car park which is basically the ground floor then you've got three sublevels below that. The BBC were parked with their satellite dish and all their communications in an office which was off to the side of the actual ramp that went up to the car park.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You've also said the other day that the mobile mortar or mortars in Sarajevo fired several times a day. That's a guess on your part, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is, but I had observers who actually saw this vehicle, I mean or vehicles running around Sarajevo doing precisely that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean I had observers --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Please stop. You've answered the question.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to object because the witness was going to add something that was relevant with regard to the extent, the area, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the question was that's a guess on your part, isn't it, answer, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that question has been answered and Mr. Ierace is free to use his time of course he could not stop if he would have asked anything else the witness should have had an opportunity to further explain. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The anti-sniping team sent into the PTT by the Presidency, having regard to your statement, was that on the 22nd of May that they came in?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea of the actual date but I know that -- I know that was -- it was very close to that because that was, I mean, a very -- the war basically started --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Please stop. Would you please look at your statement, page 6?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it highlighted.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: 22nd of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you. The correspondents who lived in Sarajevo by mid-1992 had to understand at least for reasons of their own safety, apart from any other reason, the approximate positions of the confrontation lines around the city, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The footage that you were shown by the Defence when the building close to the Holiday Inn was hit included tracer fire, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: It would have been an easy matter for, in that instance, Kate Adie, I think it was, to observe, by looking at the tracer fire, where it was coming from, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should have been but the media were limited in where they could go and I mean you've actually shown that yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Please, please, listen to this: I'm not asking where she went but what she could see and indeed what we could see indicated there was tracer fire if she was able to see along that line of tracer fire unimpeded, she should have been able to see which side of the confrontation line it was coming from, would you agree or disagree?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would only agree if she was in a very elevated position and she had full observation in order to do that and I mean she would have to be up like we were on top of the PTT where we had our observation post or she would have to be on the ridge line where we had our OP up in Papa 7. Up here.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. The -- excuse me, Mr. President. Mr. President, the Prosecution has a number of other taped excerpts with transcripts that I'd like to show to the witness. There's about 10 minutes worth and there's probably about 10 minutes worth of questions involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber allows you to do it and let's then finish then at the break so just shortly after 12:30.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: We don't have transcripts for two of those segments so I won't show those. For the benefit of the video booth can we see, can we start to watch one segment at a time, the particular videotape which had the visit by Sir Douglas Hurd, not that segment, that was the first segment on the tape but from the beginning of the second segment on that tape and I -- whilst that's being located and set up, we hand out some transcripts. Mr. President, we've been working elsewhere in the building this morning preparing transcript we simply haven't been able to -- we're still working on it but we don't have yet the transcript for the last two segments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we expected they would drop in one by one. The video director has some difficulty in knowing exactly what he is now supposed to play.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The tape is P3793 if that assists and if we could skip the first segment on that tape and commence from the beginning of the second segment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please look at the video, Mr. Gray? It's -- we are not there yet. I apologise. Could you now please look at the video, Mr. Gray? The sequence may be played, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Please pause there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you recognise the voice of Martin Bell?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you recollect if ever you knew what month it was when that interview with General MacKenzie took place?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would probably be in July.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Next segment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Again, that was Martin Bell; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Incidentally, when you were shown photographs of the tracer fire against the building next to the Holiday Inn you were asked about some holes on the side and you said they were tank rounds fired by the Serbs. Do you know why they did that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Holiday Inn was actually used by snipers --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Please stop. Not the Holiday Inn the building that was nearby that was hit by a tank?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Both of those buildings were being used by snipers. Have a look at the area around those buildings and see how high above they are and what visibility you get from them and you realise why they were being used as snipers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you recognise that building in that photograph to be the same building which we saw in the clip a minute ago?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't. I mean it looks very similar but I mean I cannot -- I mean you have to show me the clip again.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Okay. You heard a reference to the fire in the upper storeys being left to burn out. Isn't it the position that when firemen tried to put out fires in Sarajevo after the conflict broke out, and throughout 1992, that firemen would be sniped?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everyone was being sniped at.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you have a difficulty in agreeing with that question, Mr. Gray?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No I agree that they were being sniped at.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You agree by saying everyone was being sniped?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Including firemen when they were attempting to put out fires; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, we saw also a reference to a Ukranian soldier being shot dead. Even though the Sarajevans clearly had misgivings about the UN mission, it was not in their interests for the UN to withdraw completely, was it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: True. Can I make a comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: No, I suggest to you that in terms of strategy and tactics, it may well have been in the interests of the Bosnian Serb army for the UN to withdraw?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Might we now see the next clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What was the comment you'd like to make, Mr. Gray?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The UN were -- sorry and I had nothing to do with it so -- were extremely unwise in the selection of the battalions that they sent to Sarajevo. They sent a Ukranian Battalion who ethnically were linked with the Serbs and they sent an Egyptian Battalion who religiously were linked to the Muslims. They had a French Battalion there who were neutral but I mean the reason that the Ukrainians were targeted was clearly because the local population saw them as ethnically-linked to the Bosnian Serbs. That's my comment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. Gray, that assumes, of course, that the shooting was coming from the -- what you call the Muslims, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does assume that, yes, you're correct, but I mean if you have a look at the position of Marsal Tito barracks, have a look at where it is and then have a look at the ground --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, I think we're familiar with the position of the Marsal Tito barracks. Would you please now watch the next clip?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Martin Bell again?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: He said, "What made this time different was that for the first time in the city centre, some of the incoming fire," I emphasise those words, "was not directed at the government positions, the target instead was the UN Ukranian troops who were part of the UN force." Did you hear him say those words?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: His perception is that it was incoming not from within the city; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: His perception, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you hear him say those words?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now, also on that clip we saw an attack on the Presidency. When, approximately, were the Ukranian barracks destroyed, as we saw on the video, what month?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in August.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that from time to time, the Presidency was mortared?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The next clip, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I think Kate Adie that time quite clearly, she identified herself?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: She referred to fire at fight as being indiscriminate, would you agree with that, given the cover of dark?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Do you accept that if you fire at a target in a city at night if you don't have light and you don't have night vision then by its nature it's indiscriminate?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can line up targets by daytime to a fire by night and you set your weapons on fixed lines and that's how you actually determine the target and fire your weapons that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. And when you do that, it's important to check if you had lined up a legitimate target that in the meantime, civilians have not got in the way; would you agree with that or perhaps you wouldn't agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. She said that the onslaught, she called it, a Serbian onslaught is possibly in retaliation for an attempt by the Bosnian to break out from the siege in the past few days. We've heard a lot of evidence, Mr. Gray, that indiscriminate fire would often be levelled at the city seemingly in retaliation for a Bosnian either success or initiative in a military sense do you agree with that or disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: We saw a huge fire as she described it with the Bosnian national library --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace I will just let you finish this question then please pause.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And there was reference to the London conference, when was the London conference, what month?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I think it was in June.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And at that stage had the library already been shelled before the fire?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did the fire destroy it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fire did destroy it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace, the Chamber wonders whether it's of any further assistance of the Chamber to hear the comment of this witness on the clips of video. We also heard a lot of evidence that reporting was not always giving a full and -- account of everything that happened and -- but apart from that, it's mainly comment of the witness to --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, to save time, one of the remaining clips is the full version of the segment showing the tracer fire. That is -- that part which dealt with the tracer fire. I'm happy to not show that to witness but to tender it anyway so that the Trial Chamber has --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Tracer fire, what -- the clip already played before.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The Defence played part of it but not -- it didn't capture all of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, I had in mind to ask that clip be played again because I have some questions to it so perhaps we could then play the whole part, the whole clip. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. In order to save time, I think that the Prosecution has used up more time than was allocated to them now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... questions, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, I'll just check the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You took a lot of time in asking comment of the witness on these video clips and --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Well Mr. President, I'm happy to just leave it with the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is just to indicate that the way you used your time, I mean the Chamber, as you may know, does not easily stop a line of presenting evidence but here the Chamber considered that you might have been more restrictive to -- for yourself. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Can I answer that question, first, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You asked me a question may I respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please respond to the question. Mr. President, I'm happy, given what you're said, to perhaps finish by allowing the witness to view that clip again or alternatively not do that but make it available to the Bench for that fuller version to be shown to the witness during your questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, as I indicated before if it's a fuller version then we'll look at the fuller version when we see that clip. No further questions, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll adjourn until 1.00. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I interrupted you, as a matter of fact, Mr. Ierace asked if he could first respond to my question. Please respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Given the number of issues raised in the course of cross-examination and the time that remains, I am under the impression that if you have questions and I think that you will, I don't think we'll be able to round everything up in three quarters of an hour that now remain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We might not finish that and --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As a result, perhaps we could inform the witness of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gray, it might be the case that we cannot finish your testimony today.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It might be that we cannot finish your testimony today. I'm seeing that you are not quite happy with that. Would you still be available next Monday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On Monday?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's Friday today and during the weekend, we cannot sit, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I came here for one single purpose and that was to testify at this Tribunal. That was my only purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've done no sightseeing, I've doing nothing. I've just sat in my hotel room or sit in a courtroom. That's all. I will finish the job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and perhaps you might have then a bit of time during the weekend for sightseeing. We'll adjourn until 1.00. --- Break taken at 12:40 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I've been informed now by the Defence as to the subject matter of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Simply ask this question, is it really necessary to have a meeting to deal with that subject matter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I wondered whether it would be necessary but at the same time, I considered it to be better to give an opportunity to explain and if it's preferred not to be done in Court I will be glad to listen to it and see what to do then.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, would it be possible to have the meeting at a slightly later time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm looking at you, Madam Registrar. 3.00, is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since one of the legal officers and a representative of the registry will be -- will have to be present as well --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: An alternative, Mr. President, might be since we're sitting in the afternoon on Monday, that we have it on Monday morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's just hear from Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'd like to remind that I have to go to Geneva very frequently, that I'm not based in The Hague which is also the case today and we've accepted this date, this hour; however, we'd like also to seize upon this occasion to raise some other points and General Galic has just reminded me that it is very important for him also in view of his exhaustion and he has also reminded me of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At what time does your flight go, Mr. Piletta-Zanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's late afternoon, rather.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's then try to be very efficient, having lived in The Hague for some 20 years, I know approximately what the distance to Schipol airport is so we'll try to keep that in mind if you keep it in mind as well and be as efficient as possible we could have a brief meeting at 3.00. Mr. Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, could I also indicate that the fuller version of that incident we discussed earlier has not yet been transcribed, that was towards the end of the tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It might not be played by today, I'm not quite sure, but I would like to ask the parties, Mr. Gray has been in Sarajevo in a time period certainly of importance for the conflict. It is prior to the -- at least most of the time was prior to the period of the indictment. Both parties have given lengthy information, have presented lengthy information about what happened in that period, it's not for the first time that we hear information of it. Let's try not to cover whatever has been said by whomever during a period of six months, both parties have already taken a long time in respect of that so some self-restriction would not be bad. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness I do not know you still have with you but then the usher will help us if you don't, P7388. These were the fragments taken from what General MacKenzie was saying. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gray, may I ask you -- well first of all, you have a bit of problem with your -- yes, may I ask you not to mark, if not specifically asked for on any document that is in front of you because we noticed that you have made some yellow markings on other documents and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the document that was given to me yesterday. This is the one that just was given to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just the request is not to mark on the one given to you now and you should take the one given to you now in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. President, first, I will start with the real beginning and the real beginning is first to apologise to the witness and I'm very happy to do that because by mistake last night, we finished late and I took away, in my file, a document which comes from his own file and which was circulated by the Prosecution and the Defence and it is this document and I'd like to return it after you have seen it, Mr. President, I'd like it to be given back to the witness because it is one of his documents which, by mistake, some how I happened to take away.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note that I still have one of those documents as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was my second question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was looking for those documents this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. My apologies on the part of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll try to make your return into the any poorer than you came, Mr. Gray.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I thought I was going crazy I looked for these forever.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, will you please concentrate on page 457 and the last paragraph which starts with on Douglas Hurd's and so on and so forth. Will you please read that first sentence?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: "On Douglas Hurd's arrival, there were ten to fifteen members of the TDF on either side of the building's entrance as a sort of honour guard."

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. This honour guard which was therefore on both sides of the entrance had nothing to do with, I think, the line --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I haven't finished my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... was already there, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. If you didn't ask for what you were telling the witness it was not necessary. If you want to ask the witness about what you were telling him, it was leading. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will be very happy to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: The entrance of the building -- no, I'll rephrase it. Do you remember the -- those ten or fifteen men who constituted the honour guard?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us if you remember when were they constituted in relation to the incident that you spoke about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were lined up on the road at about 5, 10 metre intervals and immediately prior to the incident, they moved from, as I looked from the actual main entrance of the Presidency, they moved from left to right and the liaison officers who were standing next to me outside the front entrance actually moved inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well. Witness, you made some precisions in your testimony this morning and I believe to have understood you that you more precisely information regarding the presence or absence of General MacKenzie; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you now tell us whether, as far as you can remember, he was present or absent?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absent.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Therefore, witness, when General MacKenzie describes the situation, that is, this guard of honour that was there, as a matter of fact, he was not an eye witness, was he?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I object for two reasons. Firstly it's leading and secondly, it covers -- it adds nothing to cross-examination. There's no greyness about cross-examination on this point. The witness has already given clear evidence of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, if you want to establish that someone who is not present and that was the testimony of the witness, if he writes a book that it could not be of his own observation, I mean the Chamber is -- has sufficient intelligence available to understand such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. President. Another subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: On the other hand, and as I do not perhaps -- the Chamber is not aware also of certain techniques, for instance, Witness, you mentioned several times concerning this incident you mentioned the primary. I will ask you the following question?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: There was no cross-examination in relation to that aspect of the witness' evidence in chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, may I respond when the witness wanted to give his explanation, he resorted -- he said but there was a -- this primary and it was stopped and therefore, I am referring to what he said and that is why I'd like an opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... it was -- the primary was an issue raised in chief. If, in cross-examination, for whatever reason, further questions are put to that, you can't say that the matter has been raised in chief even if the Prosecution thought it not necessary to hear any additional observations not specifically asked for by the Prosecution. I'll allow you this question but at the same time, the Chamber will be more strict on any future question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... not go into that because of time issues. If Mr. Piletta-Zanin raises this issue now, I'd seek leave to cross-examine the witness on the issue of primaries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll change the subject with pleasure. Therefore, I'm changing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: The hearing on the 20th, you were again interrupted and we were talking about a mortar shot which hit the facade of the building that you were living in and that you told us that there were hundreds of persons living in that building and you also said the following and I quote, [In English] The civilians moved from the very front wall of the apartment building, they moved into [Interpretation] and then you were stopped at that point by the Prosecutor. Since you said that those civilians, if I understand you well, retreated, moved away from the front wall and you were about to add something, to add the more information to it, I'd like to ask you to do that now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... when the witness started and was interrupted.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The sentence -- no, I can't remember it exactly but I'd like to quote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have misunderstood my question. I'm not referring to return fire from the UN I'm saying in relation -- so the witness was stopped in giving an answer where he misunderstood the question. It's not an issue that has been raised in cross-examination, please move to your next subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, may I confer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Moved away from the front war appears in a line where the witness said, "I mean we weren't returning any fire. I mean the civilians basically moved from the very front wall of the apartment building, they moved into the" -- and then was interrupted. That was ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, but if one looks at the whole of the question as such, he was interrupted because sure, first he said we did not return fire, but the base of the question which wanted to find out whether there were any inhabitants there or not, he wanted to answer that and that information is highly valuable and I do not think it has anything to do with that. We never returned fire, but he was talking about the situation in that building at a given moment in relation to the incident of a shot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... what you've got, do you have four civilians on the other side when you returned fire if any? That was a question about civilians at the other side of the confrontation line when the fire was returned. Then the witness started telling about civilians on his own part. Then Mr. Ierace stopped him because he was not asking for that. So it's not an issue raised by the Prosecution in cross-examination. Please proceed to the next subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: On the other hand, immediately after that and I believe the Prosecution asks you a question about whether you informed the commander that a civilian -- that there were civilians in that building and after that you were asked whether the fire -- the gunfire continued and there you answered, "No, not often, two or three times." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So my question is as follows: In relation to those three or four times that you mentioned, could you tell us if, at that time, on those three or four occasions, the relevant building -- whether there were civilians still living in that building and where were those civilians if there still were there any civilians or if not, whether, perhaps, there were only the military left or were both groups of people still there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were civilians there, but they're on the -- what I would call the forward or the western side of the building. It was being used by snipers to snipe at Nedzarici, so I mean there was a combination of both but I mean my neighbours were still living in their apartment, they were on the rearward, the eastward side of the building. The westward side, the apartments had mostly been evacuated and they had moved away and they were either moved into other buildings but the westward side of my building and the other building in the actual complex were being used by snipers for -- against Nedzarici.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Can you be more precise as to the time that this happened at the very beginning or of the developments such as you knew them in Sarajevo at some other time or did it happen throughout your tour of duty in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It started at the very beginning of the war in Sarajevo or the war in Bosnia and it continued throughout it and the student hostel, what I call the student hostel, the triangular building which is marked on the map which I marked two days ago, I think, that was also being used against Nedzarici and the Serbian positions that were in Nedzarici.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. In view of the fact what you tell us after -- about this time, did you, and I'm talking about the military, did you consider the response of three or four mortar shots, did you consider it disproportionate or proportionate or what would you say about the returned fire?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Considering the amount of sniper fire and small arms fire coming from the apartment buildings that I was actually living in, it was probably proportionate.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'd like us to go back to what you told us and we are still at this building and in answering the Prosecutor, you said that those buildings were used as a kind -- as headquarters for units of combat and you spoke about young men with bandannas, with headbands indicating who they belonged to. I'm saying, I'm showing who they belonged to and therefore my question is as follows: Since there were different colours indicating different membership, can you -- affiliation, what affiliations were they, were they companies or what, did they also refer to the size of these groups, can you tell us something about that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: They showed the affiliation to companies of the Territorial Defence force, the Presidency forces. I mean there are also armoured vehicles that were in -- directly inside the apartment complex that I was in.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, it took me a moment to check the transcript. I don't see any reference to headquarters which is included -- which was included in the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Translation, translation, I never mentioned "headquarters," I heard that in English. I spoke about a combat base. I think that the term was "mounting up operation" if that can be of any assistance to my learned colleague but this is on the basis of my memory.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The term I used was forming up place, that is the term that I used. They used it as a forming-up place to actually attack towards Nedzarici.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I would like to instruct you, Mr. Gray, if a question is put to you, try to listen carefully to the question and answer that question and if there's anything else Mr. Piletta-Zanin would like to know he'll certainly ask you. You were asked about what the colours were about and I think you ended up with APCs in or next to the building. That has got nothing to do anymore with the colours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm trying to provide as much as information as I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand and we fully appreciate that but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. We'll return to the armoured vehicle. You mentioned being part of the Territorial Defence but why several colours since if one is part of the Territorial Defence it seems to me that one colour would have been sufficient?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was to differentiate between units, so I mean there were more than one unit actually working in and around our apartments.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. When you used the term "units," from a military perspective, what size are you referring to? What is the size of the unit, how many men are included in a unit?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, this goes well beyond cross-examination it goes well beyond the questions asked, the answers given.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where the specific question of units and size of units was dealt with in cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could perhaps find it again but certainly not as far as the size of units is concerned but the witness spoke about these different units and what we should be interested in is to find out whether we're speaking about number X or number Y.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... but the question was to what extent this relates to what has been raised in cross-examination not the mere fact that it has been -- but -- sometimes it's quicker. Do you know how big these units were, Mr. Gray?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. They had the blue and red and they were of approximately company size which would be 100 men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And how many would there be in that building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were -- I mean when I saw them, they were getting ready to attack Nedzarici and there were at least two companies of them so we're talking 200 men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please move to your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: The other thing is that the witness has just provided some information about an APC, may I ask him about this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and it has not come up in cross-examination. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're quite right. Thank you. I'll go back to the bombing incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You told us in order to explain your view and your conception of this incident, you said something to the effect of, "I was, myself, in the convoy or I was in an APC myself," and at that point you were interrupted. My question is what did you want to say exactly since, if I have understood you correctly, you arrived in a UN vehicle before the politician. My question is as follows: Did you have just one vehicle, did you have several vehicles when you arrived at the Presidency building?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only had one vehicle. I went by a VBL, which is one of the small APCs you can see it in the videotapes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll now go back to the incident that you refer to as involving a bomb in the market. You were asked a certain number of questions about the reasons for which you didn't establish contact with certain authorities or with certain journalists and you said that that wasn't part of your duties. I would like you to expand on that last point. I think you said that it wasn't your task?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. We were unarmed military observers. Because we had the expertise there at the time, we went to investigate the actual -- whether or not it had been caused by artillery or mortars or whatever, we considered that it was not caused by artillery or mortar, that it was actually a plain bomb that someone had placed there. We gave that information to the sector headquarters. Sector headquarters, it was then up to them to actually do any further investigation. It was not our job. We merely had the professional people who could establish what had actually hit or exploded in the actual market.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You said that at that time, there was only one crater. Are you categorical about that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am sure of it, yes. There was only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, as far as you know, what kind of calibres were used, as far as you know, by the forces that were present, this concerns mortars?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The calibres used were an 82 millimetre mortar, 120 millimetre mortar, 122 millimetre howitzer, 105 millimetre howitzer, a single barreled rocket launchers of 128, I think, millimetre, multi-barreled rocket launchers of 128 millimetre, and that was -- and small arms and heavy machine-guns. That basically covers the whole lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to examine the other incident with regard to this incident you provided with a copy of General MacKenzie's book an excerpt from this book and you were asked to have a look at certain passages where rumours were mentioned. My question is: Were these rumours widespread or were they not widespread among UN personnel? What could you tell us about this subject?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I presume you're referring --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President, again in terms of it not arising from cross-examination. He was asked specific questions about the incident and about sources of information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That is in terms of eyewitnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. The credibility of this witness has been tested at length, for example, he was told you were the only source of this information, this was one of the questions and I note that there is a text that one can read or reread here and which talks of other sources so I think that in this sense, I have the right to pursue this course of examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will not disallow you to put that question, but it took you seven lines to put that question. The question was, Mr. Gray whether in the book -- General MacKenzie talks about rumours, whether these rumours were also among your people heard.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can you -- I'm sorry, can you direct me to the specific part of the text?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, could you please assist me where exactly do you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, 456, 457 at the very end of the page. 457, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: But Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The witness has already said in cross-examination that he was the only UN person there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I think it was whether the rumours spread among UN personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And the explanation that Mr. Piletta-Zanin gave for that question for no similarity to that question, the question was about rumours how widespread. His justification was sources of information in terms of eyewitnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, is it -- do you want to establish that on the basis of rumours the witness would have had additional information? I have some difficulty in exactly finding the rumours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President, the word rumours doesn't appear in the text but at the bottom of the page, the mention was made of [In English] by the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, everyone who witnessed the event and did not the witness testify that he was the only one from the UN who witnessed the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, that was my question. I can't say this if the witness doesn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I read the last three lines, it says there was only circumstantial evidence, but everyone who witnessed the event had an uneasy feeling that it had been orchestrated, et cetera. Rumours do not appear in that part of the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with you absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... was around among UN people is not something that arises from cross-examination. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, you nevertheless said that you had spoken to General MacKenzie after this event?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I gave him a full report and this is where this came from in his book and the report was sent to the UN headquarters in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Did you speak to him directly, that is to say, did you express yourself verbally to General MacKenzie in addition to this written report?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
